title: Day 42 · Week 6, Day 0 — Body: the first look — what a six-week scan can and can't show, the heartbeat at a hundred and eleven, the measurement that can move your due date, and the risk that falls with every week it's seen
summary: Week 6 opens on the first day most practices will scan, and on the day Episode Zero promised: the day the due date — and your day number — can move. Your baby is 4–6 mm at Carnegie stage 13 (NHS: a pea with a tail): neural tube sealed at both ends, leg buds appearing under the arm buds, a looped heart starting to divide, and a face in four pieces — lens disc, closed ear pockets, a flat nasal plate and two pairs of jaw arches — that will meet over the next four weeks. What a transvaginal scan shows today: sac, yolk sac and a bright line with a flicker. The number that sounds wrong: in 2,164 pregnancies the mean embryonic heart rate was 111 bpm at days 42–45, 125 at 46–49, 145 at 50–52 and 157 at 53–56 (Stefos 1998) — so 110 is normal today. What slow actually means (Doubilet & Benson 1995 bands; Radiology 2005, 2,937 pregnancies: first-trimester loss 9.1% with a normal rate, 17.4% borderline, 60.6% slow, 77.9% very slow; slow-then-normal 25.4% vs 7.2%). No heartbeat under 7 mm CRL is a repeat scan in 7–14 days, not a diagnosis (Doubilet 2013, NEJM). M-mode, not Doppler, in the first trimester (AIUM 2020). The crown-rump length: accurate to about five days (Robinson & Fleming 1975; ACOG CO 700 ±5–7 days), and the rule — before 9 0/7 weeks, redate if the scan differs from the period date by more than 5 days, once — worked through with examples; NICE's dating scan sits at 11+2–14+1 for a reason. The risk curve after a heartbeat: 9.4% at 6 completed weeks, 4.2% at 7, 1.5% at 8, 0.5% at 9 (Tong 2008); 7.5% overall at 6–10 weeks, rising with age and falling with gestation (Makrydimas 2003) — so a six-week scan locates and counts, and the eight-week scan reassures. Safety: ACOG CO 723; Newnham's 1993 five-scan trial (RR 1.35 for birthweight <10th centile) answered by the same group's 8-year follow-up of 2,714 children in 2004 (no differences); the FDA's standing warning on home Dopplers. Twins: 30.1 per 1,000 US births (CDC 2024); chorionicity is read before 14 weeks (ISUOG, Khalil 2016) — ask 'one placenta or two' before 'identical'. The scan card: LMP and cycle length on the front, three numbers on the back.
action: One index card for the pregnancy file, next to the Day 40 question sheet, which comes to the scan. Front, filled in tonight: her last period date and usual cycle length (Day 40, question one) and the due date you calculated on Day 28. Back, three blank lines for three numbers to ask for in the room: the crown-rump length in millimetres; the heart rate, and which band it's in for the day; and the ultrasound dating in weeks and days, with the question 'does this change the due date, and by how many days?' If it does, cross out the Day 28 due date, write the new one and tonight's new day number under it, and move every dependent date in your calendar. If the scan isn't this week, fill in the front tonight and leave the back for the day. And one rule said out loud: no Doppler at home, this trimester or any other.
